solution:
\(690^\circ = 360^\circ + 330^\circ\), so \(690^\circ\) is coterminal with \(330^\circ\), which lies in the fourth quadrant where sine is negative.
Reducing about \(360^\circ\): \(\sin 690^\circ = \sin 330^\circ = \sin(360^\circ - 30^\circ) = -\sin 30^\circ\).
\(\therefore \sin 690^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(495^\circ = 360^\circ + 135^\circ\), so \(\sin 495^\circ = \sin 135^\circ\). The angle \(135^\circ\) lies in the second quadrant, where sine is positive.
Reducing about \(180^\circ\): \(\sin 135^\circ = \sin(180^\circ - 45^\circ) = \sin 45^\circ\).
\(\therefore \sin 495^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)

\(315^\circ\) lies in the fourth quadrant, where cosine is positive.
Reducing about \(360^\circ\): \(\cos 315^\circ = \cos(360^\circ - 45^\circ) = \cos 45^\circ\).
\(\therefore \cos 315^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)

\(600^\circ = 360^\circ + 240^\circ\), so \(\cos 600^\circ = \cos 240^\circ\). The angle \(240^\circ\) lies in the third quadrant, where cosine is negative.
Reducing about \(180^\circ\): \(\cos 240^\circ = \cos(180^\circ + 60^\circ) = -\cos 60^\circ\).
\(\therefore \cos 600^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(225^\circ\) lies in the third quadrant, where tangent is positive.
Reducing about \(180^\circ\): \(\tan 225^\circ = \tan(180^\circ + 45^\circ) = \tan 45^\circ\).
\(\therefore \tan 225^\circ = 1\)

Tangent is an odd function, so \(\tan(-690^\circ) = -\tan 690^\circ\).
Now \(690^\circ = 360^\circ + 330^\circ\), and \(330^\circ\) lies in the fourth quadrant where tangent is negative:
\(\tan 690^\circ = \tan 330^\circ = \tan(360^\circ - 30^\circ) = -\tan 30^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).
\(\therefore \tan(-690^\circ) = -\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\)

\(240^\circ\) lies in the third quadrant, where cosine (and hence secant) is negative.
Reducing about \(180^\circ\): \(\sec 240^\circ = \sec(180^\circ + 60^\circ) = -\sec 60^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{\cos 60^\circ}\).
\(\therefore \sec 240^\circ = -2\)

Secant is an even function, so \(\sec(-855^\circ) = \sec 855^\circ\).
Now \(855^\circ = 720^\circ + 135^\circ\), so \(\sec 855^\circ = \sec 135^\circ\). The angle \(135^\circ\) lies in the second quadrant, where secant is negative:
\(\sec 135^\circ = \sec(180^\circ - 45^\circ) = -\sec 45^\circ\).
\(\therefore \sec(-855^\circ) = -\sqrt{2}\)

\(780^\circ = 720^\circ + 60^\circ\), so \(780^\circ\) is coterminal with \(60^\circ\), which lies in the first quadrant where all ratios are positive.
\(\operatorname{cosec} 780^\circ = \operatorname{cosec} 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sin 60^\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\).
\(\therefore \operatorname{cosec} 780^\circ = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\)

Cotangent is an odd function, so \(\cot(-1110^\circ) = -\cot 1110^\circ\).
Now \(1110^\circ = 3 \times 360^\circ + 30^\circ = 1080^\circ + 30^\circ\), so \(1110^\circ\) is coterminal with \(30^\circ\) (first quadrant) and \(\cot 1110^\circ = \cot 30^\circ = \sqrt{3}\).
\(\therefore \cot(-1110^\circ) = -\sqrt{3}\)

Reduce each allied angle. \(\pi + x\) is a third-quadrant angle, so \(\cos(\pi + x) = -\cos x\); cosine is even, so \(\cos(-x) = \cos x\); \(\pi - x\) is a second-quadrant angle, so \(\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\); and \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + x\) is a second-quadrant angle taken about \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so the co-function appears with a negative sign: \(\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + x\right) = -\sin x\).
L.H.S. \(= \dfrac{(-\cos x)(\cos x)}{(\sin x)(-\sin x)} = \dfrac{-\cos^2 x}{-\sin^2 x} = \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x}\)
\(= \cot^2 x = \) R.H.S.

Reduce each allied angle. \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + x\) is a fourth-quadrant angle taken about \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), so the co-function appears and cosine is positive there: \(\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + x\right) = \sin x\). Also \(\cos(2\pi + x) = \cos x\) and \(\cot(2\pi + x) = \cot x\) (period \(2\pi\)), while \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x\) is a third-quadrant angle about \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), giving the co-function with a positive sign: \(\cot\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x\right) = \tan x\).
L.H.S. \(= \sin x \cos x\,[\tan x + \cot x] = \sin x \cos x\left[\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} + \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\right]\)
\(= \sin x \cos x \cdot \dfrac{\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x}{\sin x \cos x} = \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x\)
\(= 1 = \) R.H.S.

Reduce each angle to its coterminal angle first.
\(840^\circ = 720^\circ + 120^\circ\), and \(120^\circ\) is in the second quadrant where secant is negative: \(\sec 840^\circ = \sec 120^\circ = \sec(180^\circ - 60^\circ) = -\sec 60^\circ = -2\).
\(\cot(-945^\circ) = -\cot 945^\circ\), and \(945^\circ = 720^\circ + 225^\circ\) with \(225^\circ\) in the third quadrant where cotangent is positive: \(\cot 945^\circ = \cot(180^\circ + 45^\circ) = \cot 45^\circ = 1\), so \(\cot(-945^\circ) = -1\).
\(600^\circ = 360^\circ + 240^\circ\), and \(240^\circ\) is in the third quadrant where sine is negative: \(\sin 600^\circ = \sin(180^\circ + 60^\circ) = -\sin 60^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
\(\tan(-690^\circ) = -\tan 690^\circ = -\tan 330^\circ = -(-\tan 30^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).
L.H.S. \(= (-2)(-1) + \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\)
\(= \dfrac{3}{2} = \) R.H.S.

Reduce each allied angle. About \(90^\circ\) the co-function appears: \(\operatorname{cosec}(90^\circ - x) = \sec x\) and \(\tan(90^\circ + x) = -\cot x\) (second quadrant, tangent negative). About \(180^\circ\) the same function is kept: \(\sin(180^\circ - x) = \sin x\) (second quadrant, sine positive) and \(\sec(180^\circ + x) = -\sec x\) (third quadrant, secant negative). About \(360^\circ\): \(\cot(360^\circ - x) = -\cot x\) (fourth quadrant), and \(\sin(-x) = -\sin x\).
Numerator \(= \sec x \cdot \sin x \cdot (-\cot x) = -\dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot \sin x \cdot \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} = -1\)
Denominator \(= (-\sec x)(-\cot x)(-\sin x) = -\dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\cdot \sin x = -1\)
L.H.S. \(= \dfrac{-1}{-1} = 1 = \) R.H.S.
_note: Both numerator and denominator reduce to the constant \(-1\); the identity holds for every \(x\) for which all six ratios are defined. Verified numerically at 10 sample angles.

solution:
Reduce each allied angle. \(\sin(\pi + x) = -\sin x\), so \(\sin^3(\pi + x) = -\sin^3 x\); \(\sec(\pi - x) = -\sec x\), so \(\sec^2(\pi - x) = \sec^2 x\); \(\tan(2\pi - x) = -\tan x\); \(\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + x\right) = -\sin x\), so \(\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + x\right) = \sin^2 x\); \(\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\); and since cosecant is odd, \(\operatorname{cosec}^2(-x) = \operatorname{cosec}^2 x\).
Numerator \(= (-\sin^3 x)(\sec^2 x)(-\tan x) = \sin^3 x\,\sec^2 x\,\tan x\)
Denominator \(= \sin^2 x \cdot \sin x \cdot \operatorname{cosec}^2 x = \dfrac{\sin^3 x}{\sin^2 x} = \sin x\)
L.H.S. \(= \dfrac{\sin^3 x\,\sec^2 x\,\tan x}{\sin x} = \sin^2 x\,\sec^2 x\,\tan x = \dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}\cdot\tan x = \tan^2 x \cdot \tan x\)
\(= \tan^3 x = \) R.H.S.
_note: The last factor of the printed denominator is set as "cosec\(^2\) \(- x\)" with no bracket. Solved as \(\operatorname{cosec}^2(-x)\), which is the only reading that makes the identity true: taken literally as \(\operatorname{cosec}^2 x - x\) the equality fails at every one of 10 sample angles tested (e.g. at \(x = 0.7\) the L.H.S. is \(0.8422\) against \(\tan^3 x = 0.5976\)). Note \(\operatorname{cosec}^2(-x) = \operatorname{cosec}^2 x\), so the intended factor is simply \(\operatorname{cosec}^2 x\).

solution:
Reduce each allied angle about \(270^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\). Taking \(\theta\) acute, \(270^\circ + \theta\) is a fourth-quadrant angle and the co-function appears with sine negative there: \(\sin(270^\circ + \theta) = -\cos\theta\). Similarly \(270^\circ - \theta\) is a third-quadrant angle: \(\sin(270^\circ - \theta) = -\cos\theta\). About \(180^\circ\) the function is kept and cosine is negative in the third quadrant: \(\cos(180^\circ + \theta) = -\cos\theta\).
L.H.S. \(= \cos\theta + (-\cos\theta) - (-\cos\theta) + (-\cos\theta)\)
\(= \cos\theta - \cos\theta + \cos\theta - \cos\theta\)
\(= 0 = \) R.H.S.
